text:
===== FILE 19673__1.docx =====
September 1, 2025  

Dr. Steven L. Lieberman
Under Secretary for Health 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Avenue NW
Washington, D.C. 20420 
Submitted Electronically   
Attention: Comments in Response to Proposed Rule, RIN2900-AS31 
Dear Under Secretary for Health Dr. Lieberman:
The National Alliance to End Sexual Violence (“NAESV”) joined by the 25 undersigned national and state organizations writes to comment on the Department of Veterans Affairs (“the Department” or “VA”) Proposed Rule on Reproductive Health Services (“Proposed Rule”). NAESV is the voice in Washington for the 56 state and territorial sexual assault coalitions and 1500 rape crisis centers working to end sexual violence and support survivors.   As a committed advocate for survivors of sexual assault, NAESV and the undersigned organizations oppose the Proposed Rule, and ask the VA to recognize that reproductive healthcare is necessary for veterans, and especially necessary for veteran survivors of sexual assault.
The VA provides hospital care and medical services to veterans through the Veterans Health Administration (“VHA”) and to veterans’ spouses and dependents through the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (“CHAMPVA”).  In 2022, the Department amended VA regulations to remove the exclusion on abortion counseling and establish exceptions to the exclusion on abortions for veterans and their loved ones, including implementing exceptions for the life or health of the pregnant person and cases where the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest (the “2022 IFR”). The Department later finalized this rule in 2024 (the “2024 FR”). Although still not perfect, this policy has nevertheless been critical to ensuring that, regardless of the ever-shifting and restrictive landscape of state laws in a post- Dobbs world, the more than nine million veterans enrolled in VA’s program, as well as dependents and caregivers enrolled in CHAMPVA, would be able to access life- and health-preserving medical care.  Now, however, the VA’s Proposed Rule seeks to reinstate the pre-2022 exclusions on abortions and abortion counseling, which, if adopted, would leave veterans and their loved ones without access to abortion counseling or abortions in the case of life or health of the pregnant person and in cases where the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest.
NAESV and the undersigned organizations oppose this proposal to walk back critical reproductive healthcare for our veterans and their loved ones and disagrees with the VA’s determination that such services are “not needed.”  Ample evidence confirms it is necessary for far too many veterans and their loved ones (as the VA previously acknowledged in promulgating the 2022 IFR).  
Specifically, women veterans are at greater risk of sexual assault and intimate partner violence than their civilian counterparts. Indeed, one in three women veterans report experiencing military sexual trauma. One study even revealed alarmingly high rates of sexual harassment and assault among female veterans using Veterans Health Administration (VHA) services. Moreover, research indicates that a significant proportion of post-9/11 women veterans accessing VHA reproductive health care—approximately 68.7%—screen positive for military sexual trauma (MST), with 44.9% reporting experiences of military sexual assault.  
The Department cannot ignore these staggering figures of the frequency with which its veterans experience sexual violence, but it also should not ignore the very real health consequences resulting from that sexual assault.  According to the most recent National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey, 14.9% of female victims of rape become pregnant.  Moreover, as the Department previously found, survivors of military sexual trauma may experience significant health impacts, including PTSD, depression and other mood disorders, and substance abuse disorders. Women who are denied abortions and abortion counseling, compared to women who are able to access comprehensive reproductive services, including abortion care, are also more likely to be tethered to an abuser and to be at risk for continued violence, even if they end the romantic relationship. For the veteran and military community, this is especially troubling: the rate of spousal abuse in the military is twice as high as the rate among the national population, and the transition to civilian life may continue or exacerbate intimate partner violence. Considering these findings, it is particularly troubling that the proposed rule would explicitly rescind comprehensive health care access for survivors of sexual assault.
The proposed rule fails to contend with this evidence or otherwise explain its policy reversal.  It does not even address the rape and incest exceptions with any specificity.  Survivors of sexual violence, who have experienced the devastation of having their bodily autonomy attacked, must have access to the full range of reproductive healthcare services, choices, and options including abortion and, at a minimum, abortion counseling.  If after exploring all of her options, a veteran or veteran’s beneficiary that is a victim of any form of sexual violence decides that she cannot go through with a pregnancy resulting from the crime causing her great bodily injury and risking further injury, the VA should not further traumatize such victims by barring them from the full range of reproductive healthcare in the healthcare system that was (and currently is) promised to them.
Sincerely,
Monika Johnson Hostler, President & CEO
